headline.main: A Miracle?: Pope Francis Helps Transsexual Prostitutes in Rome
headline.social: A Miracle? Pope Francis Helps Transsexual Prostitutes in Rome

intro: The Catholic Church is not exactly known for its tolerance of transsexuals. But after a priest near Rome called the Vatican's attention to the difficulties faced by a group of transsexuals in his parish, Pope Francis stepped in to help.
text:
When the priest Don Andrea Conocchia began distributing food and medical supplies out in front of his church one day in winter 2020, a strange thing happened. Just like on the day before and, indeed, throughout the entire week, a crowd of people was lined up – 300, perhaps 400 of them.
The pandemic had just begun and Italy had come to a screeching halt. Many had already lost their jobs and help from the state was not yet forthcoming. They were hungry.
The priest of Torvaianica, a coastal town near Rome, knew almost all of those in line, or had at least seen them before. But on this afternoon, he saw a new face. In front of him was a transsexual prostitute from Argentina, looking at him shyly. "Her name was Paola,” Andrea Conocchia recalls. "Father, I beseech you,” she said, according to the priest, "can you help me like you help the others?” She received pasta and a can of tomatoes, coffee, crackers and milk. She then disappeared.
The next day, Paola was there again, and she had brought a friend along with her. The next day, there were three of them, and then four. Before long, 150 trans people were lined up in front of his church for food, most of them from Latin America. The priest and the prostitutes began talking and trust was slowly established, he says. After two or three weeks, Paola approached him with three friends. "Don Andrea, we have to pay our rent, but we don’t know how,” they told him, he recalls.
Conocchia thought about it, and then he had an idea. "You are all from Argentina, aren’t you? Just like Pope Francis?” he asked them. "Tell him about your lives in a nice letter. Tell him of your troubles. I am certain that Pope Francis will help.”
The Catholic Church does not exactly have a reputation for tolerance. It is much better known for its strict sexual morals, its discriminatory attitudes to sexual minorities and its numerous disparaging comments about people who don’t live in accordance with the church’s traditional family values. In recent months, Francis has hit the headlines twice for using homophobic slurs.
The pope, to be sure, has also sent more conciliatory, open-minded signals. But when it comes to the teachings of Catholicism, he is unyielding. In April, after five years of consultations in the Vatican, he signed a document with the title "Dignitas Infinita” or "Infinite Dignity.” Some sections of it read like a broadside against the world beyond Catholic doctrine.
Pope Francis deems gender theory to be "extremely dangerous.” It amounts to a "concession to the age-old temptation to make oneself God,” the text reads. Trans people come in for particular criticism: "Any sex-change intervention … risks threatening” a person’s "unique dignity.”
At first glance, it would seem, the pope and the trans-gender community near Rome don’t make for a good match.
Conocchia recalls that he visited Paola and her three friends at their home not long later. He was surprised that they hadn’t yet written a letter to Francis and he handed them pens and paper. "They started crying,” he says. "Don Andrea, we can’t tell the Holy Father that we are prostitutes and how we live,” they told him. "I used to have 15 to 18 clients each day, one after the other,” one of them admitted in tears.
But ultimately, Conocchia says, they started writing, drawing hearts on the paper for Francis as well. "They were tear-soaked letters,” says the priest. He collected them and sent them to the Vatican.
Torvaianica is one of several beachside towns southwest of Rome. Highways lead from the Italian capital through fields and industrial parks to the coast. It is here, on the side of the road, that the transsexuals stand, waiting for customers. They return to their homes late at night, frequently little more than shacks in a forest behind the beach with no running water, heat or electricity.
It’s a Saturday in late fall and several of them have returned to Don Andrea’s rectory. The pandemic has long since passed, but they have continued to rely on his help. Many of the prostitutes are in Italy illegally and have no health insurance. They do, however, frequently suffer from potentially serious medical issues. "They inject their breasts themselves with silicon from the building supplies store, and infections are often the result,” the priest says, describing a typical problem. On this Saturday, he is offering free medical consultations with doctors volunteering their time.
Consuelo is one of those waiting her turn in front of the mobile treatment station next to the church. "I am 53 years old. Never before has a priest spoken with me. On the contrary: They have discriminated against me. I believe in God, but I was always too afraid to enter a church.”
Consuelo has long, dark hair and is wearing lipstick along with a red necklace of glass beads. Her eyes are both serious and sad. She takes a deep breath and begins telling her life story. "When I was nine years old and discovered my sexuality, my parents in Colombia threw me out of the house. I have been living on the streets since then. I tried to get a job, but people like me aren’t hired back home. As some point, I ended up as a prostitute.”
When she was 18, she had had enough. "In Colombia, they simply kill people like me. Gay and trans people are shot dead on the street. I came to Italy to save my life.”
Her story cannot be independently verified, but those told by others waiting in front of the church are similar. They speak of the violence they faced in their South American homelands, of fleeing places like Uruguay, Argentina and Peru and of the greater degree of safety and freedom they experience in Italy. "It felt like paradise here for a long time,” says one of them.
But then came the pandemic and threw everything into disarray. "I had nothing to eat. I already had AIDS and then, when I got COVID, I went to pray in the church of Torvaianica,” says Consuelo. "I thought I was going to die.” Don Andrea, she says, provided her with food and medication. Consuelo starts to cry. "He received me with open arms.”
In the Vatican, there is a position known as the prefect for the dicastery for the service of charity, a position held by Konrad Krajewski. The Polish cardinal has one task above all others: Performing charitable acts to benefit the poor on behalf of the pope.
Conocchia wrote the prefect an email describing the financial difficulties facing the transsexuals. "The answer arrived 30 seconds later,” he says. "No problem, Andrea,” the cardinal wrote. As soon as the written requests for help arrived, he would provide his assistance. After that, Conocchia began sending letters to the Vatican every week, and money would be sent back to his parish just as often – between 200 and 500 euros per person, which he would then distribute to the prostitutes.
"They couldn’t believe it,” he says. Really? From the pope?, they said. "We want to meet him. We want to personally thank the Holy Father.”
Andrea Conocchia is 54 years old. When he is making his way through the Roman winter in his sunglasses, salt-and-pepper beard and blue down jacket, he looks quite a bit different from his conservative priestly counterparts. Meeting the trans people electrified him, he says, perhaps also because it interrupted his routine, his everyday life with church services, baptisms and funerals.
He says he is extremely touched by the fact that the early skepticism in his parish has slowly faded and that even aging churchgoers now greet the prostitutes on the street. From the fringes to the center, from the bottom to the top: Conocchia believes that the Catholic Church can change.
But how should he convince the pope to meet with Paola, Consuelo and the others? He called an old acquaintance of his, Sister Geneviève Jeanningros, in the neighboring village of Ostia. "Geneviève,” he said to her, "you are the key to the heart of Pope Francis.”
The more than 80-year-old nun has a legendary reputation in Vatican circles. Not just because, until her retirement last fall, she lived with a sister in a small trailer among jugglers and ride operators at an amusement park in Ostia. But also because of her friendship with Francis, to whom she wrote a letter quite some time ago and who has visited her home on two occasions.
The transsexuals from the beachside towns would like to meet you and thank you for your assistance, Sister Geneviève wrote her old friend, the pope. And he agreed. Since spring 2020, she or Don Andrea has headed almost weekly to St. Peter’s Square with three or four of the prostitutes to attend the general audience so that eventually, all 150 of them will have the opportunity to greet Pope Francis.
"It is always a pleasure. Never is there any prejudice from him. He blesses them and allows himself to be embraced,” says Don Andrea. He pulls out his phone to show the message with which the pope responded to the trans people. He then reads aloud what the Holy Father wrote to him, the priest from the small town of Torvaianica. "Dear Brother, many thanks for everything you are doing for the people from the LGBTQ+ community. I support you.”
"I have never experienced anything like it,” says Don Andrea. The people and their fates, he says, are more important to the pope than church doctrine. "The Holy Ghost will never again send a pope like this one.”
The priest has continued looking after his trans community. Many in the group have begun aging. Paola, the first one he met back when she was waiting in line in front of his church, has since returned to Argentina. Some of them are fighting drug and alcohol problems and are continuing to earn their money on the roadside. Others have taken jobs caring for the sick or elderly.
And then there is Angelina Diacono. She discovered her female sexuality at the age of 14 and ran away from home at 18. Now, she is 43 years old and dreams of another life. "If God wills, I would like to become a nun and help people in war zones,” she says.
It is an afternoon in November, and there is a festive mood in the Vatican. In the great audience hall next to St. Peter’s Basilica, the tables are set with flowers and fruit. A brass band plays as Francis, in his wheelchair, is pushed in to the applause of the guests.
The pope is hosting a special lunch on the occasion of the World Day of the Poor. More than 1,300 people have been invited, including Don Andrea and 43 transsexuals from his parish. Two of them have even been given a seat at the table with Pope Francis.
"It was wonderful,” says Milagros as she leaves the hall with the others after the meal. She grows melancholic for a moment as she thinks of Argentina, the homeland of both her and Francis. "For years, we were excluded, from both the church and society,” she says. "So many of us have lost their lives.”
Like a school class on a field trip, she and the others walk along the walls of the Vatican, chatting excitedly about the little gifts they received from Pope Francis. "I hope,” says Milagros, "that we will belong one day. That we will just be part of society.” They then board the bus that will take them back to Torvaianica. Back to their shacks in the forest.
